findings.title: Webhook handler does not restrict HTTP method
findings.body: The handler creates or updates credentials regardless of req.method. This state-changing webhook should reject non-POST requests; otherwise proxies or clients that send a body with other methods can trigger credential writes, and unexpected methods produce confusing parse errors.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with strict equality instead of a constant-time comparison
findings.body: The webhook secret is compared using !==. For secret validation, use a constant-time comparison such as crypto.timingSafeEqual after normalizing both values to buffers/strings, to reduce timing-based secret disclosure.

findings.title: Credential lookup-then-create can create duplicate credentials
findings.body: The endpoint does findFirst and then update/create without a transaction or unique constraint. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app can both see no existing credential and both create one, leaving duplicate credentials. Later lookups with findFirst may then choose an arbitrary row.

findings.title: Credential update does not clear the invalid flag
findings.body: When updating an existing credential, only key is written. If the credential was previously marked invalid, for example after an invalid_grant error, it remains invalid even though a new valid key was synced. The update should also set invalid: false, or otherwise validate and reset the flag when new credentials are accepted.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema does not create the intended dynamic/index validation
findings.body: The schema uses computed keys like [z.string().toString()]. This does not create a Zod index signature; it creates ordinary object properties named the schema's string representation. The intended catch-all validation for numeric expiry properties is therefore not implemented, and valid token responses may fail validation when credential sharing is enabled.

findings.title: Generic minimum schema is used for all refreshes when sync env vars are enabled
findings.body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, this helper ignores the provider-specific schema for every token refresh, even when the refresh request was made to the real OAuth provider. This can strip or reject provider-specific fields that are required for the integration to keep working.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token'
findings.body: If the parsed response has no refresh_token, the code assigns the placeholder string 'refresh_token'. OAuth refresh responses often omit a new refresh_token, meaning the existing one should be retained. This placeholder can be persisted and overwrite a valid refresh token, corrupting the credential and making future refreshes impossible.

findings.title: Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response while many callers expect provider-specific parsed objects
findings.body: In credential-sharing mode, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT. Many call sites still expect the original provider response shape: Google expects an object with .data, HubSpot expects a token object, and Zoho callers expect an AxiosResponse with .data. This mismatch causes runtime failures or invalid token persistence when syncing is enabled.

findings.title: Google credential refresh persists the Zod SafeParse wrapper instead of the parsed key
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod SafeParse result, but GoogleCalendarService assigns that result to key and writes it to prisma.credential.key. The stored credential becomes an object like { success, data } instead of the actual token object. Subsequent parsing of credential.key will fail, breaking Google Calendar authentication. The code should persist the parsed data, not the SafeParse wrapper.

findings.title: Google token refresh assumes a provider response shape that sync mode does not provide
findings.body: After refreshOAuthTokens, the code reads res?.data.access_token and res?.data.expiry_date. In credential-sharing sync mode, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, which has no .data property. This will throw or store undefined token values when the sync endpoint is used.

findings.title: HubSpot refresh treats sync fetch Response as a parsed HubSpot token object
findings.body: When credential syncing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, but this code treats the result as a HubspotToken object and reads expiresIn. A fetch Response has no expiresIn, so expiryDate becomes NaN and the credential is updated with invalid token data.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin refresh assumes AxiosResponse .data, which sync mode does not return
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response when credential syncing is enabled, but this code accesses tokenInfo.data.error as if the result were an AxiosResponse. This will throw a TypeError because fetch Response objects do not have a .data property.

findings.title: Zoho CRM refresh assumes AxiosResponse .data, which sync mode does not return
findings.body: refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response when credential syncing is enabled, but this code accesses zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error as if the result were an AxiosResponse. This will throw a TypeError because fetch Response objects do not have a .data property.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh bypasses the credential sync endpoint
findings.body: Unlike the other modified adapters, Salesforce's getClient calls Salesforce's token endpoint directly and never uses refreshOAuthTokens. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are configured, Salesforce tokens are therefore not refreshed from the self-hosted source of truth, breaking the intended credential-sync contract for this app.

findings.title: Salesforce client refreshes the access token on every construction
findings.body: getClient unconditionally calls the Salesforce token endpoint whenever the service is constructed, without checking whether the existing access token is still valid. This adds an extra token refresh for each use of the Salesforce integration and can cause unnecessary latency and rate-limit pressure.

findings.title: Salesforce token refresh checks response.statusText instead of response.ok
findings.body: The code treats any response whose statusText is not 'OK' as an error. HTTP/2 and some fetch implementations may return an empty statusText even for successful responses, and other successful statuses may not use 'OK'. This can make valid token refreshes fail. Use response.ok instead.

findings.title: Salesforce CalendarService uses prisma without importing it
findings.body: prisma.credential.update is called in this file, but prisma is not imported. This will fail TypeScript compilation or cause a runtime ReferenceError when the Salesforce calendar service refreshes credentials.

findings.title: Salesforce credential update can lose provider-specific fields such as instance_url
findings.body: The credential key is replaced with accessTokenParsed.data plus the old refresh_token. When credential sharing is enabled, parseRefreshTokenResponse uses a generic minimum schema that does not preserve Salesforce-specific fields such as instance_url. Persisting the reduced object can corrupt the credential and break later Salesforce connections.

findings.title: Salesforce connection is created with the stale access token after refresh
findings.body: After refreshing and persisting the new access token, the jsforce Connection is constructed using credentialKey.access_token from the old credential object instead of the newly parsed access token. The refreshed token is therefore not used for subsequent Salesforce API calls.

findings.title: Outbound credential sync request has no authentication
findings.body: The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends calcomUserId and appSlug but does not include a shared secret, signature, or other authentication header. The remote endpoint has no built-in way to verify that the request originated from this Cal.com instance.
